Introduction

The Family Story

In 1837, a family well-established for generations in a rural German village sold their mill, picked up roots, and emigrated to America. Johannes and Katharina Bauer were each about 50 years old when they crossed the Atlantic with their seven living children ranging in age from seven to 25 years. The family settled in the rural town of Tiverton, Ohio. Over five generations their descendants spread throughout much of the United States.

The story of this family is presented in two volumes:

Volume 1: A Family Story portrays the family life in Germany, why they chose to emigrate, their voyage to America, their new life in Ohio, and what became of their descendants over the generations.

Available in pdf format at https://archive.org/details/bauerkleinfamilyvol1

Volume 2: Descendants Listing (this volume) provides a list of the descendants with their life events and relationships.

Available in pdf format at (xx this is the old 2021 version) https://archive.org/details/bauerkleinfamilyvol2

Available as a web page at xx TBDhttps://stevebower.github.io/BauerKleinFamily/

The Ancestry.com Repository

Ancestry.com serves as the source repository for this listing of descendants, in the “Hemlock” family tree. Anyone can access the online tree as described in Volume 1, section “Online Family Tree at Ancestry.com.” Once you have a free or paid account you can access Johannes “John” Bauer, patriarch of this family tree, with this link.

The online family tree includes much more information than found in this listing:

  • birth/death/marriage certificates, and many other documents
  • census records and images, showing where people lived during their lives
  • person fact types not included here, e.g., Residence facts showing where they lived, etc.
  • photographs and stories of many individuals
  • obituaries and newspaper articles
  • many other family relatives, including cousins and spouses' families
  • ability to browse the family tree
  • sources used to identify all persons and their relationships to others.

Not all descendants in the Ancestry.com tree are included in this listing. The Ancestry.com tree includes some possible descendants with only speculative records or relationships—such persons are not included here. As well, those born after 1980 were generally excluded from this listing, unless requested to be included by themselves or their close relatives.

Accuracy and Completeness

I have striven for diligence in establishing the relationships of married couples, and of children to their parents (including by adoption). In general, I have established relationships only where there is substantial evidence based on reliable or multiple sources. The sources for life events and relationships are all included in the Ancestry.com tree.

The facts included for each descendant in this volume are a subset of the Ancestry.com family tree, as described in the previous section. For example, this listing might include only a Marriage License fact for a married couple, with no marriage date. A marriage license alone would not mean the couple necessarily married, but for this case the Ancestry.com tree has additional facts confirming they married (e.g., an obituary referring to the marriage).

Some facts are qualified with "possible match," indicating uncertainty. For example, the following sentence indicates that it's uncertain if the record applies to this person, given the multiple names used in the record:

"Death: 22‑May‑1994. POSSIBLE MATCH: Social Security application has name listed as: Jerry Eugene Townsend (May‑1957); Jerry Lebron Gilmer (Jan‑1959); Eugene Townsend (May‑1994)."


DNA Kinship

Some descendants have a “DNA Kinship” fact, when relationships have been confirmed through DNA testing. These are for DNA matches between a descendant and the author, Steven T Bower. In all cases, the relationship predicted by the DNA match agreed with the relationships in this family tree.

Although these are for relationships to the author, they are useful for confirming the relationships between the DNA match back to the common DNA ancestors with the author.

There are three types of DNA Kinship facts for a descendant:

  • DNA Match: the descendant and the author have DNA in common
  • Common DNA Ancestor: an ancestor in common for a DNA Match and the author, by which they are related
  • DNA Connection: the descendant is in the lineage between a DNA Match and a Common DNA Ancestor.

Conventions

Numbering Scheme

Each direct descendant (biological or adopted) has a main, numbered entry that includes the lineage of ancestors leading back to the family patriarch, Johannes “John” Bauer.

For example, in the following main entry for John C Bower, his father was Jacob Bauer in generation 2, and Jacob’s father was Johannes “John” Bauer in generation 1:

14. John C Bower. (Jacob Bauer-2; Johannes "John" Bauer-1)

A main entry will describe a descendant’s spouses, but a spouse will not have a main entry.

Within a main entry, children are listed with their main entry numbers, with the birth order shown by Roman numerals (i, ii, iii, ...). Children without a known or estimated birthdate are listed first, regardless of the actual birth order. For example:

Children of Isabell "Belle" Darling and John C Bower

57i.Lemon Darling Bower. Lemon Darling was born on 21‑May‑1882 in Bethlehem, Coshocton, Ohio. He died on 17‑Apr‑1961 in Mansfield, Richland, Ohio. He married Mabel V Sharpless in 1905 in Coshocton County, Ohio.

58ii.Ward James Bower. Ward James was born on 18‑Sep‑1884 in Bethlehem, Coshocton, Ohio. He died on 7‑Dec‑1923 in Bethlehem, Coshocton, Ohio. He married Goldia Mae Speckman on 2‑Aug‑1911 in Coshocton County, Ohio.

Descendant Names

Variations in the spelling of names was common, even in official documents, up to the early 1900s. Where multiple spellings were possible, the most-used spelling from early in a person’s life is generally used. For example, Johannes and Katherina’s first son, Jacob Bauer, was often referred to as Jacob “Bower” as an adult in census records and legal documents. Jacob’s children are all listed herein with the surname “Bower”.

Women are listed by their birth (maiden) names.

Unknown names are shown as "______", often for maiden names.

Alternate or uncertain names are shown in brackets, for example:

  • “Klein [ Kline ]” for an inconsistent spelling,
  • “Klein [ Smith ]” for someone born Klein but adopted by the Smith family
  • “[ Johnson ]” for a woman’s surname when it’s uncertain if it’s her birth name.

A first name of “[ Infant ]” is for an infant who died with no known name.

Location Names

To better reflect the historical context, place names reflect the time of the recorded events. For example, a person born in Kansas in 1860 would have a birth place of “Kansas Territory” since Kansas became a state in 1861. Many counties and towns have changed their boundaries or names over time. I have tried to use the correct names for the times of recorded events, noting the current name where needed for clarity.


The “Town, County, State” convention within the United States

All locations in the United States are in the form: Town, County, State.

For example:

Coshocton, Ohio= Coshocton County, Ohio
Coshocton, Coshocton, Ohio= Coshocton City in Coshocton County, Ohio
Kansas City, , Missouri= Kansas City, county unknown, Missouri

The “town” may be a township, town, city, village, or other local community. The least specific place should be assumed — for example, “Keene, Coshocton, Ohio” refers to Keene Township, not Keene Village within the township.

Some place names include “County” for clarification (e.g., “Mississippi County, Arkansas”), but this is inconsistent. The “Town, County, State” format is consistently used for locations in the United States.


Event Dates

The accuracy of the dates provided is only as good as the sources from which they were determined. When different sources had different dates (not unusual), I made every effort to use the date of the most reliable source(s). For example, a birth date on a death certificate would generally take precedence over a birth date on a headstone.

A date will be “about” when uncertain due to its source(s), or when estimated from other events.

For some of those born more recently (e.g., after the 1950 U.S. Census), a birthdate may be based on public residence or phone records, generally supported by an approximate birthdate (e.g., based on their age in years in a census or marriage record). In these cases, “about” is used even when a full birthdate is provided, as in “about 23 May 1957”, given the occasional inaccuracy of dates in public residence/phone records.

Abbreviations

Common abbreviations include:

b.born
m.married
d.died
abtabout

Marriage Order

Marriages and non-spousal relationships are listed in chronological order, generally even when a marriage date is unknown (e.g., if the marriage order can be inferred from the children’s ages, or a divorce record).

Johannes "John" was born on 20‑May‑1788 in Steinbach am Donnersberg, , Palatinate, Kingdom of Germany. He died in Feb‑1860 in Tiverton, Coshocton, Ohio at the age of 71 years, 8 months. He was buried in Probably: Tiverton, Coshocton, Ohio. He was the son of Johann Jakob Bauer and Maria Katharina Becker.

He married Katharina "Catharine" Klein in 1811.
